item.title: When AI Gets Cheaper, Do Prices Follow? Information Delays and Algorithmic Pricing
item.description: arXiv:2610.31693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine whether lower costs of running AI models lead to lower prices, and whether delays in observing competitors' prices and limits on price changes affect how much consumers benefit. We study a simulated market with two differentiated sellers, logit demand, and tabular Q learning. A factorial experiment varies the age of rival price information, how often sellers can revise prices, whether production costs fall, and differences in firm quality and costs. We evaluate policies trained on 60 paired market seeds in each of 16 conditions, for 960 training runs, and measure expected consumer surplus after learning ends. In the main setting with identical firms and falling costs, the estimated interaction between information delay and repricing frequency on consumer surplus is -0.00025 normalized units, with a 95% paired seed bootstrap interval of [-0.0402, 0.0393]. The interval includes zero, as do intervals for tests of whether the interaction changes with the cost regime or differences between firms. With the shortest information delay and the ability to revise prices every period, average price reductions equal 55.6% and 44.0% of the imposed cost reduction for the two firms. Mean consumer surplus under the learned policies is below the corresponding static grid Nash benchmark in all 16 conditions. The findings show that simulated cost savings need not be fully passed on to buyers. They do not establish collusion or describe pricing by actual AI providers.
item.dc:creator: Krish Tadigotla

item.title: Jawboning the Fed: Do Markets Listen When Administrations Talk?
item.description: arXiv:2610.32300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide the first systematic evidence on whether financial markets price political pressure on the Federal Reserve as a signal of future monetary policy. Using approximately four decades of Reuters newswire articles from 1988 to 2025, classified by an open-weight large language model ensemble into dovish and hawkish pressure, we estimate the daily response of interest rate expectations across the term structure, the US dollar, inflation compensation, and market volatility. Dovish pressure lowers near-term rate expectations by roughly one basis point per pressure event---equivalent to a four-percent increase in the implied probability of a rate cut at the next FOMC meeting---with the effect decaying monotonically and vanishing beyond the three-month horizon. Hawkish pressure has no detectable effect. Furthermore, excluding the Trump presidencies does not weaken the estimate, ruling out the possibility that the result is confined to an idiosyncratic recent episode. The response is accompanied by dollar depreciation, with stable inflation compensation and market volatility. We interpret the pattern as markets pricing anticipated monetary accommodation, rather than a credibility tax on the nominal anchor.
item.dc:creator: Michela Baretti, Umberto Collodel, Jacopo Zacch\'e

item.title: AI-Augmented Research: Free to Write, Costly to Read
item.description: arXiv:2610.32355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a model in which artificial intelligence lowers the cost of writing faster than the cost of reading. Authors differ in reputation, and time-constrained readers, such as referees, choose between ignoring, verifying, and trusting papers. As writing costs fall, the band of verified papers shrinks: outsiders are no longer read, and established authors are no longer checked. In the ``costless writing limit,'' the share of verified papers vanishes, and a paper's impact depends on its author's reputation alone. Readers can escape the flood by asking AI to summarize the literature. These summaries aggregate papers reliably only if their errors are sufficiently independent. Once the share of papers written with the same AI exceeds a threshold, summaries inherit the AI's errors, and AI review filters out the original research that could correct them.
item.dc:creator: Wolfgang Kuhle

item.title: Delayed Retirement, Intergenerational Transfers, and Fertility
item.description: arXiv:2610.32455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Population aging and fertility decline are occurring simultaneously worldwide, straining labor supply and pension systems. China began a gradual delayed-retirement (GDR) reform in 2025, raising statutory retirement ages on different schedules for men, female cadres, and female workers across birth cohorts. To evaluate its effects on older individuals and within the family, we develop a model of older adults' retirement, intergenerational transfers, and adult children's fertility decisions, with parameters estimated via fuzzy regression discontinuity at the pre-2025 statutory retirement ages. Counterfactual simulations show that, for mature reform cohorts, the GDR reform increases older employment and monetary transfers to adult children but reduces grandparental childcare. Because the reduction in childcare outweighs the increase in monetary transfers, fertility and older adults' welfare decline, with particularly large losses among lower-income women. Fully flexible retirement, mandatory partial retirement, and mandatory full-time work do not raise employment without similarly reducing fertility and welfare. Childcare subsidies can offset the declines in fertility and welfare, while restricting eligibility to women or lower-income women requires higher subsidy rates but reduces average fiscal expenditure. These findings suggest that evaluations of retirement policy should consider not only its direct effects on older adults' labor supply, but also its fertility effects through intergenerational transfers; childcare support can help mitigate these negative intergenerational effects of delayed retirement.
item.dc:creator: Yi Fan, Shuangshuang Song, Yewen Yu

item.title: Blameocracy: Causal Rhetoric in Politics
item.description: arXiv:2504.06550v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Democratic politics requires voters to infer how political actions map into outcomes, yet these causal links are often unclear, giving politicians scope to shape voters' causal accounts. This paper studies the supply and returns of causal rhetoric in politics: politicians' language linking political actions to outcomes through blame and credit. We fine-tune a language model to measure its use in 4.2 million congressional tweets spanning 2012--2023. Causal rhetoric is central to politicians' communication: it accounts for more than one third of tweets, is the language of political disagreement, and rises over time. The political returns of causal rhetoric are concentrated in blame. Combining campaign contributions with quasi-exogenous geographic variation in Twitter adoption, we find that exposure to blame has the largest effects on small donations. Using voting intentions from survey data and an event-study design around blame-only and credit-only days, we find that politicians' support rises after blame-only days. Finally, causal rhetoric appears rarely supported by economic knowledge, particularly blame.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Bilotta, Alberto Binetti, Giacomo Manferdini

item.title: GenAI-Assisted Writing and Academic Performance: Evidence from the Social and Behavioral Sciences
item.description: arXiv:2510.02408v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies how Generative AI (GenAI)-assisted writing is associated with peer-reviewed publication output and journal placement in the social and behavioral sciences. We select lexical markers whose frequency rose sharply after ChatGPT's release in late 2022 and classify authors as GenAI-assisted writers when the share of these markers in their papers' titles and abstracts rises relative to their own pre-release baseline. Using matched author-level panel data and a difference-in-differences design, we estimate a 72% increase in publication output among GenAI-assisted writers relative to matched comparison authors in 2025. Across alternative specifications, the estimates range from roughly 52% to 88%. Mean journal placement based on the SCImago Journal Rank (SJR) improves by roughly 1%, but this modest increase is less consistent across different specifications. Within authors' annual publication portfolios, the highest placement improves by 5%, whereas the lowest declines by 3%. However, only the improvement at the top persists once the annual number of publications is held constant. The increase in output is accompanied by an expansion of collaboration networks and a rise in single-authored publications. Productivity gains are largest among early-career researchers and authors from countries linguistically distant from English, groups likely to face greater writing-related barriers to publication. The results suggest that GenAI-assisted writing may lower these barriers and increase researchers' capacity to bring more projects to publication.
item.dc:creator: Dragan Filimonovic, Christian Rutzer, Conny Wunsch

item.title: Short-Run Multi-Outcome Effects of Nightlife Regulation in San Juan
item.description: arXiv:2510.25782v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: I evaluate San Juan, Puerto Rico's late-night alcohol sales ordinance using a multi-outcome synthetic control that pools economic and public-safety series. I show that a common-weight estimator clarifies mechanisms under low-rank outcome structure. I find economically meaningful reallocations in targeted sectors -- restaurants and bars, gasoline and convenience, and hospitality employment -- while late-night public disorder arrests and violent crime show no clear departures from pre-policy trends. The short post-policy window and small donor pool limit statistical power; joint conformal and permutation tests do not reject the null at conventional thresholds. I therefore emphasize effect magnitudes, temporal persistence, and pre-trend fit over formal significance. Code and diagnostics are available for replication.
item.dc:creator: Jorge A. Arroyo

item.title: Carbon Regulation and Competition in the European Airline Industry
item.description: arXiv:2603.27724v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The European Union Emissions Trading System is set to substantially increase the effective carbon price faced by airlines. We estimate a two-stage model of airline competition with endogenous product entry, direct departure frequencies, and pricing. Impacts are highly asymmetric across carrier types and market segments. Consumer surplus declines by up to 34% overall and up to 95% in medium- and long-haul markets. Short-haul markets gain welfare as airlines reallocate capacity toward shorter routes. Airline profits decline by 1--42%, but carbon tax revenue of $1.9--2.9 billion and the social value of avoided emissions of $2.7--4.0 billion more than offset private-surplus losses.
item.dc:creator: Ertian Chen, Lichao Chen, Lars Nesheim

item.title: Execution and Evaluation: Task Content, Labor Demand, and the Evaluator Pipeline
item.description: arXiv:2607.20807v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Measures of occupational AI exposure ask whether machines can perform a task, not which function the human supplies. I distinguish execution, producing a first-pass output, from evaluation, judging whether it is correct, and make the distinction measurable by scoring all 19,265 O*NET task statements under fixed rubrics. The execution score is reproducible across model coders and O*NET vintages. In a 200-task random audit it correlates 0.81 with the mean of four blinded human coders. It predicts each held-out coder's peers better than that coder does, though the coders disagree substantially among themselves. It adds only modest power beyond O*NET's evaluation activities. Employment growth is lower in execution-heavy white-collar occupations in every window since 2012; the gradient shows no post-2022 break and lies largely between occupational families. The Eloundou exposure gradient is steeper in 2022--2025 than in the pandemic window, but the design does not establish an AI effect. A near-term seniority test is null. If evaluative judgment is itself produced by execution practice, the supply of evaluators falls only after a cohort lag; that prediction remains untested.
item.dc:creator: Li Gan

item.title: BeforeIT.jl: High-Performance Agent-Based Macroeconomics Made Easy
item.description: arXiv:2502.13267v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: BeforeIT is an open-source software for building and simulating state-of-the-art macroeconomic agent-based models (macro ABMs) based on the recently introduced macro ABM developed in [1] and here referred to as the base model. Written in Julia, it combines extraordinary computational efficiency with user-friendliness and extensibility. We present the main structure of the software, demonstrate its ease of use with illustrative examples, and benchmark its performance. Our benchmarks demonstrate that the base model built with BeforeIT is orders of magnitude faster than its original Matlab implementation, while achieving performance comparable to a highly optimised HPC implementation. Furthermore, we show how BeforeIT supports an easy construction of model variants such as the 'CANVAS' model of [2], how these variants can be evaluated at scale via an automated multicountry forecasting pipeline, and how the entire simulation can be automatically differentiated. BeforeIT is designed to facilitate reproducibility, extensibility, and experimentation. As the first open-source, industry-grade software to build macro ABMs, BeforeIT can significantly foster collaboration and innovation in the field of agent-based macroeconomic modelling. The package, along with its documentation, is freely available at https://github.com/bancaditalia/BeforeIT.jl under the Apache 2.0 license.
item.dc:creator: Adriano Meligrana, Mitja Devetak, Steven Hoekstra, Oliver Reiter, Enrico Minnella, Sebastian Poledna, Marco Bardoscia, Aldo Glielmo
